rv.q: Horwood's version succeeds in simultaneously teasing and taking seriously the original.
This hugely enjoyable new Sherlock Holmes adventure from playwright Joel Horwood gives you all you could possibly want from The Great Detective.
Rollicking mystery with an erratic Holmes
The commitment is undeniable, the pay-off more questionable.
In the end, though, the evening is a triumph of style over content.
Because this is a muddle from start to finish, the action progressing in fits and starts and the characters and the language showing no internal logic.
A real must-see show taking you on a journey of mystery and intrigue with the magic of Theatre.
There is originality here aplenty in an evening that looks and sounds tremendous.
Seldom can a character portrayed as often as Holmes on stage and screen, been vested with such energy.

This is a real humdinger of a Holmes, an intoxicating swirl through the mind of the fictional detective who has fascinated figures as diverse as Harrison Ford, Agatha Christie, and the Sultan of the Ottoman Empire.
A bit of silliness in a serious world of doom and gloom is a wonderful thing.

The design is indeed rather more subtle than some of the writing which has the obviousness of a hammer blow, and a plot that twists and turns bewilderingly before ending up where Holmes enthusiasts might always have guessed it would land.

The narrative is frustratingly frantic, heavy on shouty exposition and with few witty lines, taking in political revolutions, stolen government documents, jail breaks, drug-addled sequences, and escaped zoo animals, with little opportunity to breathe, let alone grip with its storytelling.
There is some fun to be had in this energetic production, but it can’t make up for lazy writing and plotting.
Overall this is a fantastic new imagining of Sherlock Holmes that truly brings the intrigue of the detective to brilliant life on stage.

This is a genuinely interesting addition to the many versions of Holmes the 21st century has already produced, executed with theatrical flair and anchored by a lead performance that more than justifies the commission.

It's a romp, an excuse to indulge in a comic book version of Victorian England, a slice of Conan Doyle fan fiction that you'd have to have a heart of stone not to warm to, even as the temperature plummets.
The entire chaotic caper gets away with it thanks to a plot that trades enjoyably on the under-estimation of both women and 'the natives'.

cn.t: An ambitious, visually spectacular production divides critics with its madcap energy and postcolonial themes. Strong performances and staging can't overcome chaotic plotting and breathless pacing for some, while others embrace its cerebral irreverence.
